questions.question: After completing the ROB simulation, what is the main benefit of having a large Reorder Buffer?

answers.b: More instructions can be in-flight, increasing parallelism

explanations.a: ROB size doesn't directly affect clock speed
explanations.b: Correct! A larger ROB allows more instructions to be issued and pending, enabling better utilization of functional units and higher instruction-level parallelism
explanations.c: Larger ROBs typically increase power consumption
explanations.d: ROB size doesn't simplify decode logic

questions.question: Based on your simulation experience, when does an instruction get removed from the ROB?

answers.a: As soon as it finishes execution
answers.b: When its result is needed by another instruction
answers.c: When it reaches the head of ROB and commits successfully
answers.d: After a fixed number of cycles

explanations.a: Instructions remain in ROB after execution until commit
explanations.b: Results can be forwarded while instruction stays in ROB
explanations.c: Correct! Instructions are removed only when they reach the head of ROB and commit in program order
explanations.d: Removal is based on program order, not timing

questions.question: From your simulation observations, what happens to ROB entries when an exception occurs?

answers.b: Only the faulting instruction is removed
answers.c: Instructions before the exception commit, younger instructions are flushed

explanations.a: Not all entries are cleared; older instructions may still commit
explanations.b: Younger instructions must also be handled to maintain correctness
explanations.c: Correct! Instructions older than the exception can still commit normally, but all younger instructions must be flushed to maintain precise interrupt semantics
explanations.d: Exceptions require special handling and pipeline recovery

questions.question: Based on the simulation timeline you observed, why might an instruction stay in the 'Complete' state for multiple cycles?

answers.a: The functional unit is still busy
answers.b: It's waiting for older instructions to commit first

explanations.a: Once complete, the functional unit is freed
explanations.b: Correct! Completed instructions must wait for all older instructions to commit first, maintaining program order for commits
explanations.d: Memory bandwidth affects execution, not post-completion waiting

questions.question: In your simulation, how does register renaming interact with the ROB?

answers.b: ROB entries serve as temporary register names until commit
answers.c: Register renaming replaces the need for ROB

explanations.a: They work closely together in modern processors
explanations.b: Correct! ROB entries act as physical register names, allowing multiple instructions writing to the same logical register to coexist without conflicts
explanations.c: Both mechanisms are needed and work together
explanations.d: ROB handles all types of instructions, not just memory operations

questions.question: From analyzing the commit log in your simulation, what can you conclude about instruction commit order?

answers.a: Instructions commit in execution completion order
answers.b: Instructions commit based on their execution time
answers.c: Instructions always commit in original program order
answers.d: Instructions commit randomly to maximize throughput

explanations.a: Commit order differs from completion order to maintain correctness
explanations.b: Execution time doesn't determine commit order
explanations.c: Correct! The ROB ensures that regardless of execution order, instructions commit in the original program sequence to maintain program semantics
explanations.d: Random commit order would violate program correctness

questions.question: What performance metric from your simulation best indicates ROB effectiveness?

answers.b: ROB utilization percentage and average CPI

explanations.a: Clock frequency is determined by circuit design, not ROB efficiency
explanations.b: Correct! High ROB utilization indicates good instruction-level parallelism, and lower CPI shows performance improvement from out-of-order execution
explanations.c: Cache performance is separate from ROB effectiveness
explanations.d: Memory bandwidth is not directly related to ROB performance

questions.question: Based on your simulation experience with dependencies, which scenario would benefit most from ROB and out-of-order execution?

answers.a: A sequence of dependent instructions with long latencies
answers.b: Independent instructions with varying execution times

explanations.a: Dependent instructions can't execute out-of-order, limiting ROB benefits
explanations.b: Correct! Independent instructions with different latencies can execute out-of-order, maximizing functional unit utilization and overall throughput
explanations.c: Mixed instruction types provide more opportunities for parallelism
explanations.d: Mixed instruction types provide more opportunities for parallelism

questions.question: From your advanced simulation scenarios, what is the main challenge in implementing large ROBs in real processors?

answers.b: Hardware complexity, power consumption, and access time

explanations.a: ROB implementation is transparent to software
explanations.b: Correct! Large ROBs require complex tracking logic, consume significant power, and may increase access latency, creating engineering trade-offs
explanations.c: OS is generally unaware of ROB implementation details
explanations.d: Compilers don't need to be aware of specific ROB sizes
